document.title: Comments of Calibrant Energy requesting clarifications of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s proposal filed on 08/13/2026
document.group: PJM Large Load definition, Registry and Interim Resource Adequacy Service

pages.text:
1 
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
) 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
) 
Docket No. ER26-3515-000 
) 
 
COMMENTS OF CALIBRANT ENERGY 
 
Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (Commission) 
Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 Calibrant Energy (Calibrant) respectfully submits these 
comments requesting clarifications of PJM Interconnection, LLC’s (PJM) proposed revisions to 
its Open Access Transmission Tariff (Tariff) and the Reliability Assurance Agreement Among 
Load Serving Entities (RAA) to establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service (IRAS) rules and 
procedures.2 Calibrant seeks only a narrow subset of clarifications to provide the regulatory 
certainty needed to ensure that the IRAS proposal incentivizes the entry of any and all resources 
that are able to help address PJM’s resource adequacy challenges.  
Calibrant develops energy generation and storage assets throughout the United States, 
including in the PJM footprint. Calibrant participated in PJM’s stakeholder process to ensure that 
 
1 18 C.F.R. § 385.211. 
2 Throughout these comments, Calibrant requests that aspects of PJM’s filing be clarified to 
address ambiguities in the proposed Tariff and RAA revisions, so as to provide greater clarity to 
market participants. As explained herein, Calibrant understands these requests to be consistent 
with the policy direction intended by PJM and communicated to stakeholders in the PJM 
stakeholder process. Calibrant believes that these clarifications can be made by PJM directly, in 
this docket or otherwise, and respectfully submits that such sua sponte clarification would be the 
most straightforward and efficient option. However, to the extent PJM determines that sua sponte 
clarification is not practicable, or otherwise does not affirmatively provide such clarification, 
Calibrant directs its requests to the Commission on the grounds that, as further discussed in these 
comments, the PJM proposal risks unjustness, unreasonableness, and undue discrimination 
absent the requested clarifications. To that end, Calibrant notes that PJM “consents to the 
Commission’s exercise of authority to modify and/or sever any element of the proposed Tariff 
and RAA language to the extent necessary and permitted.” Transmittal Letter at 9.

2 
behind-the-meter energy storage projects (with or without generation)—which are new “steel-in-
the-ground” assets capable of reliably serving the long-term capacity needs of the region with a 
faster development timeline than front-of-the-meter new capacity resources—are fully eligible to 
provide Bring Your Own New Capacity (BYONC) by supporting Demand Resource 
participation.  
Calibrant supports PJM’s proposal to allow loads to avoid IRAS exposure via Demand 
Resource BYONC. Calibrant appreciates PJM’s engagement during the stakeholder process and 
PJM’s recognition of the potential for behind-the-meter projects to help address the region’s 
resource adequacy challenges. Inclusion of Demand Resource BYONC eligibility is fundamental 
to the IRAS proposal’s ability to incent bilateral contracting to bring new capacity online in a 
non-discriminatory manner. To ensure that PJM’s proposal incents as much entry of new capacity 
on the system as possible, however, Calibrant seeks clarification of several aspects of PJM’s 
proposal, which, as drafted, increase contracting risk and would accordingly discourage 
investment. Specifically, Calibrant requests clarification that: 
• Incremental Demand Resource capacity at sites that are currently providing or 
have previously provided capacity, enabled by registration of new on-site 
generation or storage installations, is eligible to provide BYONC; 
• New Large Loads and the BYONC that they contract with satisfy their obligations 
under the IRAS framework by providing capacity for the 10-year duration of the 
BYONC’s Reliability Pricing Model (RPM) obligations; 
• The demonstrations over the 10-year period that Demand Resources providing 
BYONC are required to make need only be made on an installed capacity (ICAP) 
basis.

3 
Providing these clarifications will increase regulatory certainty for potential developers, thereby 
facilitating greater BYONC participation and reducing the need for involuntary IRAS 
curtailment. They will also ensure comparable treatment across similarly situated resource types, 
incentivizing the entry of any and all resources that are able to help address PJM’s resource 
adequacy challenges. 
Calibrant also recognizes that PJM’s IRAS framework contemplates continued 
coordination with the states to ensure faithful, effective, cost-minimizing implementation. In 
particular, clear and consistent retail tariff treatment, which resides within the clear jurisdiction 
of the states, is paramount to reducing contracting risk between New Large Loads and potential 
BYONC developers, thereby encouraging entry of new capacity onto the system to address 
resource adequacy challenges. Calibrant stands ready to support those efforts.  
I. 
REQUIRED CLARIFICATIONS 
A. 
Calibrant requests clarification that incremental Demand Resource capacity 
at prior-participating locations may provide BYONC. 
PJM proposes to allow Demand Resources or DER Capacity Aggregation Resources to 
serve as BYONC under two circumstances: (1) the Demand Resource or DER Capacity 
Aggregation Resource is composed of locations that did not previously support a Capacity 
Resource (or participate as Peak Shaving Adjustment or Price Responsive Demand), or (2) the 
Demand Resource or DER Capacity Aggregation Resource is composed of “any location not 
registered in or prior to the 2026/2027 Delivery Year at which an incremental amount at that 
location is the result of the registration of new generation or storage assets at the location” (at 
least until the capacity market restabilizes, resetting the deadline from which prior-participation 
is measured).3 This second participation pathway is not clear. In order to give this provision 
 
3 Proposed Attach. DD-4 § VI(b)(ii) (emphasis added).

4 
independent effect and based on PJM’s position in stakeholder discussions, Calibrant believes 
that PJM intended this provision to allow prior-participating Demand Resources and Distributed 
Energy Resource (DER) Capacity Aggregation Resource to offer incremental BYONC capacity 
where enabled by registration of new generation or storage resources at the location. Clarifying 
this intent will incent the new entry of reliable capacity supported by new behind-the-meter 
resources and avoid otherwise unnecessary involuntary curtailment exposure. In addition, 
Calibrant requests clarification that the “incremental amount” of Demand Resource capacity 
supported by installation of new behind-the-meter resources will be measured against the 
Demand Resource’s most recent participation level.  
Absent such clarification, PJM’s proposed second qualification pathway for Demand 
Resources is confusing.4 It is not clear how new generation or storage could provide incremental 
capacity at a location that has never before participated. “Incremental” usually would imply 
additional capacity on top of existing capacity. Otherwise, it would just be new Demand 
Resource or DER capacity, not incremental capacity. Moreover, such new Demand Resource or 
DER capacity can already participate under PJM’s other proposed participation pathways for 
locations that have not previously participated in the PJM capacity construct—whether or not 
supported by new generation or storage. To give the incremental participation provision 
independent meaning, it must allow for some form of participation that adds to the other option, 
i.e., at some locations that have participated in the RPM in prior Delivery Years. Thus, the most 
natural reading of the language is that the limit on prior year registration is a bar on BYONC 
qualification only to the extent underlying storage and generation assets previously supported the 
registration (i.e., where such storage and generation is not new). Where the storage and 
 
4 See id. § VI(b)(ii)(1).

5 
generation enable incremental, previously-unregistered capacity, such capacity should be clearly 
eligible to serve as Demand Resource BYONC. 
Stakeholder conversations with PJM staff and PJM’s marked tariff redline included as 
Attachment A to its filing help to square this circle. In discussions with Calibrant, PJM staff 
explained that it intended to allow Demand Resources at locations that had previously 
participated in the PJM capacity market if new behind-the-meter generation or storage 
investments enable additional incremental Demand Resource capability. PJM’s marked tariff 
redline suggests potential confusion as to how best to provide for this result: the redlines, which 
are supplied in two different colors, suggest that a second author may have revised this proposal 
from a requirement that Demand Resource BYONC could “be composed of, or reliant on, any 
location registered in the 2026/2027 Delivery Year at which an incremental amount at that 
location is the result of the registration of new generation or storage assets at the location” to one 
where Demand Resource or DER BYONC may only be composed of “any location not 
registered in or prior to the 2026/2027 Delivery Year . . . .”5
 
 
5 PJM Transmittal, Attachment A, Revisions to the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff and 
Resource Adequacy Agreement (Marked/Redline Format), at Proposed Attach. DD-4 § 
VI(b)(ii)(1) (pdf page 100) (emphasis added).

6 
Calibrant respectfully asks for clarification that this insertion is not intended to prohibit 
Demand Resources that previously participated in the RPM from providing BYONC by 
installing reliable, steel-in-the-ground behind-the-meter storage or generation resources to enable 
additional demand flexibility. Clarifying proposed Tariff Attachment DD-4 section VI(b)(ii)(1) in 
this way will allow existing large commercial and industrial customers that have previously 
provided Demand Resource capacity but that can increase their capabilities by installing new 
behind-the-meter resources to be part of the solution to PJM’s historic resource adequacy 
challenges. Such an all-hands-on-deck approach is consistent with PJM’s goals in the IRAS 
filing of encouraging New Large Loads to cover their needs by bringing their own new capacity 
to the market.  
To the extent necessary, Calibrant requests that the Commission direct PJM to revise its 
proposed Tariff to provide this clarification on the basis that the provision as drafted is (1) unjust 
and unreasonable because it is unclear6 and (2) unduly discriminatory or preferential because it 
would exclude resources that are similarly situated to new front-of-meter generation and storage 
assets in their ability to allow New Large Loads to mitigate the region’s resource adequacy crisis 
by bringing their own new capacity. The Commission could require such modifications while 
accepting the remainder of PJM’s proposal given PJM’s express notice “that it consents to the 
 
6 See Boston Edison Co., 98 FERC ¶ 61,292, at P 21 (2002) (The Commission “has an interest in 
ensuring that tariffs clearly, completely and unambiguously identify services, rates and terms and 
conditions. The Commission thus frequently rejects proposed tariff language as unclear”); 
cf. Dominion Energy Mktg., Inc., 155 FERC ¶ 61,121, at P 21 (2016) (“We find that the lack of 
clarity regarding the process for new incremental capacity and existing capacity at the same 
resource to participate in the [Forward Capacity Auction] fails to provide reasonable notice to 
market participants of the requirements, and is therefore, unjust and unreasonable.”); see 
also PJM Interconnection, 137 FERC ¶ 61,108 (2011); Entergy Serv. Co., 106 FERC ¶ 61,039 
(2004); Toledo Edison Co., 78 FERC ¶ 61,013 (1997); Detroit Edison Co., 77 FERC ¶ 61,279 
(1996).

7 
Commission’s exercise of authority to modify and/or sever any element of the proposed Tariff 
and RAA language to the extent necessary and permitted . . . where such modification and/or 
severance is consistent with PJM’s overarching objectives in this filing.”7 Allowing incremental 
Demand Resource capacity to qualify as BYONC where facilitated by new generation or storage 
assets at locations that have previously registered would further PJM’s broader objectives by 
encouraging steel-in-the-ground investments to increase the amount of capacity that existing 
Demand Resources can reliably provide, reducing the need for involuntary curtailment. 
In addition, Calibrant requests clarification of how PJM will determine the baseline 
against which it will measure the “incremental amount” of Demand Resource capacity that a 
behind-the-meter investment allows at a prior-participating location if that Demand Resource’s 
participation has decreased from prior levels. Calibrant believes that this provision should be 
read to allow a prior-participating Demand Resource that has since deactivated, reduced its 
participation, or experienced UCAP degradation to provide capacity incremental to its most 
recent level of participation by installing new behind-the-meter resources. Measuring 
incremental additions in this way would produce a result similar to PJM’s proposal to allow 
repowered generation facilities to provide BYONC8 because it would allow a Demand Resource 
that “deactivated” to provide BYONC in the full amount of its capacity enabled by new behind-
the-meter assets, like the BYONC eligibility of a repowered generator that is credited for 
BYONC purposes based on its full capacity value and not only for capability above its prior 
capacity. For example, take a load that previously provided 50 MW of Demand Resource 
capacity but then withdrew from capacity market participation, providing 0 MW in the most 
 
7 Transmittal Letter at 9.  
8 See Proposed Tariff, Attach. DD-4, § VI(b)(i)(4).

8 
recent Delivery Year. If that load then registered a new behind-the-meter battery to provide 100 
MW of Demand Resource capacity, PJM should treat the Demand Resource as providing 100 
MW of incremental capacity and therefore 100 MW of BYONC—like the storage asset would be 
treated if interconnecting in front of the meter—rather than only 50 MW of incremental capacity.  
Measuring the incremental amount of capacity enabled by behind-the-meter investments 
from the most recent non-participation baseline will provide a clearer incentive to invest in 
behind-the-meter projects and renew participation, reducing the need for involuntary curtailment. 
Crediting incremental contributions enabled by behind-the-meter investments only to the extent 
that they exceed the maximum amount previously offered would conversely substantially mute 
existing and deactivated Demand Resources’ incentives to invest in this needed capacity.  
B. 
Calibrant requests clarification that a New Large Load and BYONC’s 
obligations under the IRAS program extend at most only through the required 10 
years of RPM participation. 
PJM proposes to require that “BYONC that is in an arrangement with a New Large Load 
must remain in such arrangement with that New Large Load unless and until the New Large 
Load is permanently out-of-service.”9 Calibrant seeks clarification, based on PJM’s statements in 
its transmittal letter and other parts of the proposed Tariff, that this tariff proposal is meant only 
to prohibit BYONC transferability and not to suggest that a BYONC must remain in service for 
the life of the New Large Load that it serves.  
PJM explains in its transmittal that it proposes to require a BYONC to remain in an 
arrangement with its New Large Load for the life of the load to effectuate its “propos[al] that 
once the subject of an arrangement[,] BYONC cannot change to a different New Large Load—
i.e., BYONC is non-transferable.”10 That is, proposed Tariff Attachment DD-4 section VII(e) is 
 
9 Id. § VII(e). 
10 Transmittal Letter at 64.

9 
meant only to prohibit a BYONC resource from later serving another New Large Load, and not 
to require a BYONC serving a New Large Load to remain in service for the lifetime of the 
load—a requirement that no new resource could reasonably commit to.  
Under this reading, the term through which the BYONC is responsible to cover the New 
Large Load’s registered peak load instead extends only to, at maximum, the 10-year period 
during which the BYONC is subject to capacity must-offer requirements under proposed Tariff 
Attachment DD-4 section VIII(b).11 This reading accommodates PJM’s express 
acknowledgement in its proposed Tariff that sellers of Demand Resources and DER Capacity 
Aggregation Resources BYONC may replace their BYONC capacity with other qualifying 
BYONC for the remainder of the original BYONC’s 10-year RPM Auction participation 
commitment.12 Replacing a resource for RPM purposes would not be reconcilable with a reading 
of proposed Tariff Attachment DD-4 section VII(e) that requires a given BYONC to remain in an 
arrangement with the New Large Load for the life of the load unless the load has retired 
unusually early. 
Calibrant therefore respectfully requests clarification that a BYONC’s duty to remain in 
service under the proposed Tariff extends only to the duration of its RPM must-offer 
responsibilities. Put differently, “once BYONC is in an arrangement with a New Large Load”—
and BYONC completes its RPM must-offer obligations under proposed Tariff Attachment DD-4, 
section VIII, “the New Large Load gets the benefit of ‘bringing’ this new capacity to the system 
and permanently reduces its availability to provide Interim Resource Adequacy Service by the 
 
11 Proposed Tariff, Attach. DD-4 § VIII(b); see also id. §§ VIII(e) & (f) (referencing Attach. DD-
4 § IV(b)(iii)) (relieving BYONC their must-offer obligations if the RPM clears sufficient 
capacity for three consecutive Delivery Years). 
12 Id. § VIII(e).

10 
ICAP equivalent of the BYONC.”13 This time-bounded, 10-year RPM must-offer requirement 
was established in the stakeholder process as a practical solution to allow for commercially 
workable bilateral contracting. While Calibrant intends to operate its behind-the-meter assets 
supporting load response for their 20+ year useful lives, Calibrant cannot commit its assets to 
operate for the duration that the load it serves remains in service. This clarification is therefore 
needed to provide regulatory certainty that a New Large Load must only contract with a BYONC 
resource for a definite term to procure protection from IRAS curtailment exposure, as opposed to 
potential indefinite exposure that could last decades and would create substantial risk for 
developers. To the extent that the Commission believes that PJM must clarify its proposed Tariff 
language to make clear that proposed Tariff Attachment DD-4 section VII(e) only prohibits 
transferring a BYONC and does not require the BYONC to remain in operation for the life of the 
load, Calibrant requests that the Commission find PJM’s proposal unjust and unreasonable given 
its conflict with the provision allowing Demand Resource and DER BYONC to be replaced in 
the RPM and direct PJM to clarify the language on compliance.14 
C. 
Calibrant requests clarification that a Demand Resource’s 10-year 
demonstration obligation applies on an ICAP basis and, for New Large Load 
Demand Resource, does not apply in Year 1. 
PJM proposes to require Demand Resources to demonstrate their availability each year 
during a 10-year period. For the avoidance of doubt, Calibrant requests confirmation that these 
demonstrations are to be made on an ICAP, rather than Unforced Capacity (UCAP), basis. In 
 
13 Transmittal Letter at 64-65.  
14 See id. at 9 (consenting “to the Commission’s exercise of authority to modify . . . any element 
of the proposed Tariff and RAA language to the extent necessary and permitted under FPA 
section 205 and NRG Power Marketing, LLC v. FERC, where such modification and/or 
severance is consistent with PJM’s overarching objectives.” (citation omitted)); see also sources 
cited in supra n.6, in which the Commission rejected confusing or unclear tariff proposals.

11 
addition, Calibrant requests confirmation that New Large Load Demand Resources are not 
required to make such an installed capacity demonstration in year 1. 
PJM proposes that a Demand Resource’s or DER Capacity Aggregation Resource’s 
Accredited UCAP shall be the Accredited UCAP for the RPM Auction in which the BYONC 
cleared for the initial Delivery Year that the BYONC is in an arrangement with the New Large 
Load.15 Further, PJM proposes to require that the Demand Resource’s or DER Capacity 
Aggregation Resource’s “Accredited UCAP . . . must be demonstrated each year for a 10-year 
period using the Demand Response or DER Capacity Aggregation Resources installed capacity 
for the first Delivery Year after the BYONC is in an arrangement with the New Large Load.”16 
Calibrant reads this requirement to require a Demand Resource to demonstrate its 
ongoing BYONC eligibility in the Accredited UCAP amount of the first Delivery Year that it 
contracts with the New Large Load using its ICAP rather than its UCAP. This reading is 
consistent with conversations with PJM staff in the stakeholder process. It also parallels the 
requirements that front-of-meter assets face in being subject to an RPM must offer requirement 
under the proposed Tariff and Tariff Attachment DD § 6.6, which requires all of the installed 
capacity of existing generation resources to be offered in all RPM Auctions for each Delivery 
Year.17 Calibrant requests this confirmation for the avoidance of doubt given potential confusion 
 
15 Proposed Tariff, Attach. DD-4 § VII(i)(ii). 
16 Id. (emphasis added). 
17 Proposed Attach. DD-4 § VIII(b) (“All BYONC in an arrangement with a New Large Load 
must be offered into the RPM Auctions as Capacity Resources consistent with and pursuant to 
the capacity must-offer requirements and exceptions set forth in Tariff, Attachment DD, sections 
6.6 and 6.6A.”); OATT ATT DD.6.6, OATT ATTACHMENT DD.6.6 Offer Requirement for 
Capacity Resour (3.0.0), § 6.6(a) (“To avoid application of subsection (h) below, all of the 
installed capacity of all Existing Generation Capacity Resources located in the PJM Region shall 
be offered by the Capacity Market Seller that owns or controls all or part of such resource (which 
may include submission as Self-Supply) in all RPM Auctions for each Delivery Year” (emphasis 
added)).

12 
in the proposed tariff as written stemming from the requirement to demonstrate the Accredited 
UCAP using “installed capacity.” This clarification will provide regulatory certainty to Demand 
Resource and DER Capacity Aggregation Resource developers that their BYONC eligibility will 
not degrade in subsequent Delivery Years, creating uncertainty that would otherwise discourage 
bilateral contracting of new demand side and distributed BYONC. 
In addition, PJM proposes that, “For Demand Resources or DER Capacity Aggregation 
Resources that are also the actual New Large Load, there is no demonstration required for the 
initial Delivery Year only to not be an Eligible New Large Load.”18 Calibrant requests 
confirmation that this means that a New Large Load that serves as its own BYONC by 
registering as a Demand Resource is not required to make an installed capacity demonstration in 
the first Delivery Year that it is participating as a Demand Resource, and is only required to make 
the demonstration in years 2-10.  
 
 
 
Respectfully submitted, 
/s/ Kim Smaczniak
